summary: Prices on the dashboard are Friday Nov 13 closes (prices_as_of 2026-11-13); Monday's session has not opened, so every level below is a Friday close unless it says premarket. Before the open, Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 1.2% and S&P 500 futures about 0.5%, while the 10 year eased to 5.14% (Seeking Alpha via TradingView). The selling is about AI, not rates: TSMC closed down nearly 6% in Taipei and AMD, ENTG and SEI traded 5% to 6% lower premarket (Traders and Quants; TradingView). New since Sunday: the administration plans to name Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Anthropic as 'national champions' (WSJ report), the Fed counted over $3 trillion of AI commitments off balance sheets, and the FAA ground stop's cause is still open, with HPE and LHX lower premarket. The put screen found nothing liquid enough, so research/put_ideas.json stays empty. Stand aside until Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close.

signals.title: Chip suppliers fall harder than Nvidia before the open; the AI names on the long term scan buy list are under their buy points premarket
signals.what_happened: TSMC closed down nearly 6% in Taipei on Monday and chip names led Asia lower (Traders and Quants). Before the US open, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 1.23%, NVDA about 3% to 4%, and AMD, Micron and Intel more than 5% (Seeking Alpha via TradingView). TradingView premarket quotes: AMD 500.52 (-6.28%), ENTG 140.00 (-5.03%), SEI 60.26 (-5.56%), ANET 190.50 (-3.44%), ADI 387.26 (-2.69%), SNPS 450.99 (-0.92%). Mizuho cut its NVDA target to $220 from $250 and TD Cowen to $200 from $275, both keeping Buy (Dow Jones; TradingView). A petition to bring Jensen Huang back has more than 177,000 signatures, and two investors asked the board not to rush a replacement (Reuters). Elon Musk wrote that many Nvidia supply deals were 'a handshake with Jensen'; no supplier or filing backs that (Traders and Quants).
signals.so_what: The market is pricing the leadership gap as a supply chain risk: suppliers build plants around Nvidia's orders, so doubt about those orders hits them first. That is why ENTG and TSMC fall harder than NVDA. Tuesday's call matters as much for suppliers as for Nvidia: if interim CEO Colette Kress can point to signed, long term orders, the extra supplier discount has little reason to stay. What would make this wrong: a weak outlook, which would turn a leadership discount into a demand problem for the whole AI compute map.
signals.for_you: Long term: AMD (500.52 premarket) is under its 525.17 point and near its 498.91 stop; ENTG (140.00) is under 147.51; SEI (60.26) is under its whole zone (61.75 to 68.95). A premarket print is not a close, but no first tranche in AMD, ENTG, ANET, SEI or ADI today or before Nvidia reports. Puts: none on these names this week. Swing: no AI setups are live.

signals.title: Washington plans to name Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Anthropic as 'national champions'
signals.what_happened: The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that the administration plans to name more than two dozen AI companies, including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, as US 'national champions' (Seeking Alpha and Reuters via TradingView). Named companies could get faster export licenses, government help abroad and access to federal financing. Commerce Secretary Lutnick could announce it as early as this week, and separate rules to stop chips going to China are also being prepared. Commerce received 78 applications under the AI exports program started by a July 2025 executive order.
signals.so_what: Federal financing and fast export licenses lower the cost of selling AI abroad for the named firms, which matters most for cloud and model companies that sell full packages overseas. It does not fix the Nvidia leadership question, and tighter anti diversion rules can cut the other way for chip sellers. The timing lines up with Thursday's Trump, Xi and Putin meeting, so expect China to answer. What would make this wrong: the list slips, or the financing turns out small.
signals.for_you: No action. MSFT stays 'Wait' (523.88 on Nov 13; up/down volume under 1.0) with a ready long term point at 519.00; it goes ex dividend Nov 19. Watch for the Commerce announcement and for any China response on Thursday.

signals.title: The Fed counted over $3 trillion of AI promises off balance sheets; Nvidia's $500 billion financing plan has no deals yet
signals.what_happened: The Fed's November financial stability report, released after Friday's close, put public debt tied to AI computing above $1.1 trillion. Signed leases that have not started top $1 trillion, and take or pay deals and resale value guarantees add more than $2 trillion, none discounted (Traders and Quants; Markets Digest). The Fed noted that GPU makers 'often provide a guaranteed residual value' on chips pledged as collateral. Bloomberg reported Nov 12 that Nvidia's plan with six investment firms, Apollo among them, to raise $500 billion of outside money has closed no deals; partners want a bigger backstop. Nscale's amended IPO filing says it has no binding financing yet for Anthropic contracts worth up to $44.6 billion (Markets Digest). The high yield spread was 3.20% on Nov 12.
signals.so_what: The risk sits in guarantees and leases more than in today's loans. A resale guarantee ties a chip maker's balance sheet to the price of its own used chips, so a falling chip market can reach lenders through collateral. Credit is calm for now; the first sign of stress would be a data center lease default or wider spreads on chip backed debt. History rhymes with 2000, when equipment makers lent to their own customers (see the cycle card).
signals.for_you: No action. APO has a ready long term point at 121.98 (123.47 on Nov 13); it is a named partner in the Nvidia plan, so wait for Tuesday's call before any first tranche. Watch the high yield spread: a move well above 3.20% while chips fall would make this a credit story.

signals.title: FAA ground stop: the fault is still open between L3Harris and HPE; Duffy asks Congress for $50 billion today
signals.what_happened: Friday's nationwide ground stop was traced to sites in Texas and Arkansas where FAA contractor L3Harris had just installed new routers from Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Officials have not decided whether the install, the setup or the hardware failed; HPE says its device worked as configured, and the FAA sees no sign of a cyberattack (Seeking Alpha via TradingView). 12,462 flights were canceled Friday and thousands more over the weekend. Transportation Secretary Duffy sends Congress a $50 billion emergency request today, up from the $30 billion he sought before. Premarket, HPE was 45.76 (-5.24%) and LHX 262.00 (-3.80%), while airlines were only 1% to 1.5% lower (TradingView; Traders and Quants).
signals.so_what: The market is charging the network owner and the router maker more than the airlines that lost the flights. Fault decides who pays. For L3Harris it cuts both ways: it may carry blame now, but it owns the network a $50 billion upgrade would rebuild, so we leave it off both lists until a cause is named. If the finding blames the install, most of HPE's discount has no reason to stay.
signals.for_you: No action. HPE has a ready long term point at 45.58 (48.29 on Nov 13) and is already near it premarket; do not buy a stock falling on an open fault question, wait for a close and the FAA finding. LHX is on the long term watch list with no buy point: under a falling 200 day (298.83).

cycle.big_cycle: Technology and external order are the active forces. Technology: the AI build is now funded partly by guarantees from the chip makers themselves. External order: a 'national champions' plan for US AI firms days before the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting.

history.what: Equipment makers lent to the carriers that bought their gear; Lehman put Lucent's customer financing commitments at $7.2 billion in early 2000 (CFO magazine), and vendor finance portfolios took large losses when carriers failed (Euromoney).
history.lesson: When a supplier funds its own customers, sales look stronger than the demand behind them, and the losses show up in the guarantees first.

history.when: February 1994 to February 1995: the Fed's surprise tightening
history.what: The Fed doubled its target from 3% to 6% in a year and US bond losses reached about $600 billion by late 1994 (Fortune).
history.lesson: Weak auctions and rising long yields came before the stock pain; Wednesday's 20 year sale is the next auction test.

cycle.differences: Telecom carriers were mostly small, highly indebted startups. Today's AI buyers include the largest, most profitable companies in the world, and the Fed says credit spreads are calm at 3.20%. The weak link this time is the newer cloud and data center firms like Nscale that have contracts before funding.
cycle.for_you: Swing: stand aside until Tuesday night; TMO is the only setup. Puts: nothing passed today; the bar is about 5.14% a year. Long term: no first tranche in AI group names until after Nvidia's report; GD, AEP and PFE are the non AI names on the buy list, and AEP has the best backtest.

principle.text: Look for the second and third order consequences, not just the first (paraphrase of Principles).
principle.applied: The first order story is Nvidia's CEO. The second order story is the suppliers whose plants depend on its orders, and the third is the lenders behind leases backed by its resale guarantees. That is why ENTG fell more than NVDA this morning.
